references.text: God commands Moses to build a sanctuary so He can dwell (שָׁכַן) among the people. The verb ἐσκήνωσεν ("pitched His tent/tabernacle") in [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14] directly alludes to the Hebrew שָׁכַן and the tabernacle (mishkan). The Word became flesh and "tabernacled" among us, just as God took up residence among His people in [ref:2 Mos 25:8-9|Exodus 25:8-9].

Moses asks to see God's glory (כָּבוֹד), but no one can see God's face and live. In [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14], John testifies that the disciples beheld the glory of the Word (δόξα) – a glory that was inaccessible in [ref:2 Mos 33:18-22|Exodus 33:18-22] is now revealed in the incarnate Son.

The Lord reveals Himself to Moses as full of grace (חֶסֶד) and truth/faithfulness (אֱמֶת). The phrase πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας ("full of grace and truth") in [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14] directly reflects this self-revelation in [ref:2 Mos 34:6|Exodus 34:6].

The Lord's glory (כָּבוֹד) fills the tabernacle. John uses the tabernacle motif when he says that the Word "pitched His tent" among us and that we beheld His glory ([ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14]), in line with [ref:2 Mos 40:34-35|Exodus 40:34-35].

The prophecy of the virgin who will conceive and bear a son, Immanuel ("God with us"). The incarnation in [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14] – that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us – is the fulfillment of the promise that God Himself would be with His people ([ref:Jes 7:14|Isaiah 7:14]).

The Lord's glory will be revealed, and all flesh shall see it. [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14] declares that this glory has now become visible in the incarnate Word, in accordance with [ref:Jes 40:5|Isaiah 40:5].

The Lord promises to come and dwell (שָׁכַן) among His people. [ref:Sak 2:14|Zechariah 2:14] points forward to the fulfillment in [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14], where the Word takes up residence among humanity.
God sent His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh. Paul confirms the same truth as [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14]: the Word/Son truly became flesh (σάρξ) – [ref:Rom 8:3|Romans 8:3].

Christ, who was in the form of God, took the form of a servant and became like men. The Christ hymn in [ref:Fil 2:6-8|Philippians 2:6-8] expresses the same movement as [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14]: from divine glory to human flesh.
"The mystery of godliness is great: He was revealed in the flesh." [ref:1 Tim 3:16|1 Timothy 3:16] confirms the incarnation proclaimed in [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14]: the Word became flesh.

John testifies concerning the Word of life, which we have heard, seen with our own eyes, and touched with our hands. [ref:1 Joh 1:1-2|1 John 1:1-2] expands on the eyewitness testimony mentioned in [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14]: "we beheld His glory".

Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. [ref:1 Joh 4:2|1 John 4:2] makes the incarnation from [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14] a decisive criterion for confession of faith.

God has spoken to us in these last days through His Son, who is the radiance of His glory. [ref:Hebr 1:1-3|Hebrews 1:1-3] emphasizes that the Son's glory (δόξα) is God's glory – the same that John beheld in [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14].

Jesus identifies His body with the temple. The incarnation in [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14] – that the Word "tabernacled" among us – is further explained in [ref:Joh 2:19-21|John 2:19-21], where Jesus' body is the new temple.

God loved the world so much that He gave His only Son (μονογενής). The phrase μονογενοῦς παρὰ πατρός in [ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14] is expanded upon in [ref:Joh 3:16|John 3:16], which explains the purpose of sending the only Son.

Jesus asks to be glorified with the glory he had with the Father before the world began. [ref:John 17:5|John 17:5] confirms that the glory the disciples saw in [ref:John 1:14|John 1:14] is the eternal glory the Son shares with the Father.

God, who said, 'Let light shine out of darkness,' has shone in our hearts to give us the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Jesus Christ. [ref:2 Cor 4:6|2 Corinthians 4:6] connects God's glory (δόξα) with revelation in Christ, as [ref:John 1:14|John 1:14] testifies.

Zion is called to rejoice, for the Lord comes and will dwell among his people. [ref:Zech 2:10|Zechariah 2:10] points forward to God's presence among humanity, an expectation fulfilled in [ref:John 1:14|John 1:14].

God's dwelling (σκηνή) is with humans, and he will dwell (σκηνώσει) among them. [ref:Rev 21:3|Revelation 21:3] uses the same tabernacle verb as [ref:John 1:14|John 1:14] and points to the perfect fulfillment of God's presence among his people.

For it was God's will that all fullness should dwell in him. [ref:Col 1:19|Colossians 1:19] emphasizes that God's fullness took up residence in Christ, a parallel to [ref:John 1:14|John 1:14], where the Word became flesh, full of grace and truth.

For in him dwells all the fullness of deity bodily. [ref:Col 2:9|Colossians 2:9] confirms the incarnation: God's full being lives in Christ in bodily form, as [ref:John 1:14|John 1:14] testifies that the Word became flesh.
